text: Yes, there is water on the Moon, but you couldn't swim in it. It comes in two main forms. Near the poles, ice is hidden in deep [[crater|craters]] that never see sunlight. Across much of the surface, tiny amounts of water are trapped inside the dusty soil and rocks.

Scientists confirmed this in 2009. India's [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-1]] spacecraft carried a NASA instrument called the Moon Mineralogy Mapper, which spotted the chemical signature of water and related [[molecule|molecules]] spread over the Moon's surface. The same year, a NASA probe called LCROSS crashed into a dark crater near the south pole and found water in the cloud of dust it kicked up.
How much ice there is, and where it came from, are still big questions.

st.prompt: Why might water ice survive in some craters near the Moon's poles, but not near its equator?

options.t: The crater floors never get any sunlight
The poles have a thick atmosphere

st.reveal: The Moon's axis is barely tilted, so near the poles the Sun always skims low on the horizon. The floors of deep craters stay in permanent shadow and very cold, so ice that lands there can stay frozen for billions of years.

sec.t:
When the Apollo astronauts brought back [[@apollo-moon|Moon rocks]] between 1969 and 1972, scientists tested them and found almost no water. Many concluded that the Moon was completely dry.

New tools changed that. In 2008, scientists re-examined tiny beads of volcanic glass from Apollo samples and found traces of water inside them. Then came Chandrayaan-1. Its Moon Impact Probe and NASA's mapper both picked up signs of water in 2008 and 2009.

In 2020, NASA's SOFIA, a telescope flying inside a jumbo jet, found water molecules even in a sunlit crater. The amount was tiny, roughly a small bottle's worth spread through a cubic metre of soil. The Sahara Desert holds far more.

There are several ideas, and the answer may be all of them. [[@comets|Comets]] and some [[asteroid|asteroids]] carry ice, and crashes could have delivered it. The [[@solar-wind|solar wind]] brings hydrogen from the Sun, which can join with oxygen in Moon rock to make tiny amounts of water. Ancient volcanoes on the Moon may also have released water from inside.

Each source leaves a slightly different chemical fingerprint, so scientists hope future samples will settle the question.

Water is heavy, and launching it from Earth is very expensive. If future astronauts can dig up ice on the Moon, they can melt it to drink and use it to grow food. Splitting water gives oxygen to breathe. Hydrogen and oxygen are also the ingredients of powerful [[@rockets-how|rocket]] [[@rocket-fuel|fuel]].

That is why the Moon's south pole has become a popular target. In 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 landed closer to the south pole than any spacecraft before it. In 2024, a US lander called Odysseus touched down even closer. NASA's Artemis programme plans to send astronauts to the same region, and other countries are planning missions there too. The ice in those dark craters may one day work like a petrol pump for spacecraft heading further into the solar system.

text: The planets come in two very different sizes. The four inner planets, [[@mercury-planet|Mercury]], [[@venus-hot|Venus]], Earth and Mars, are small and rocky. The four outer planets, Jupiter, Saturn, [[@uranus-sideways|Uranus]] and Neptune, are giants made mostly of gas, liquid and ice.

[[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]] is by far the biggest. It is about 11 times as wide as Earth, and about 1,300 Earths could fit inside it. All the other planets put together would fit inside it too. Mercury is the smallest, a little more than a third as wide as Earth. Earth is the biggest of the rocky planets, but next to the giants it is tiny.

myth: The planets are fairly close together, like the pictures in books.
Book pictures squash the planets together so they fit on a page. Real distances are huge compared with the planets' sizes. Most of the solar system is empty space.
facts: Earths that could fit inside Jupiter

sec.t:
Mercury, the closest to the Sun, is barely bigger than our Moon. Venus is almost Earth's twin in size, only about 5% narrower, but its thick air makes it the hottest planet. Mars is about half as wide as Earth, yet it has the [[@space-weird-tallest-mountain|tallest volcano known in the solar system]]. Olympus Mons rises about two and a half times higher than Mount Everest.

All four have solid surfaces you could stand on, with mountains, valleys and [[crater|craters]]. In old Indian astronomy, Mars is called Mangal, Venus is Shukra and Mercury is Budh. Some days of the week in Hindi are named after them, like Mangalvar for Tuesday.

Beyond Mars and the [[asteroidbelt|asteroid belt]] lie the giants. Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium, the same gases that make up the Sun. Neither has a solid surface to land on. Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been swirling for at least 150 years. Go down into their clouds and the gas just gets thicker and hotter.

Saturn is the second-biggest planet, about nine times as wide as Earth. Yet it is so light for its size that, on average, it is less dense than water. That's where the bathtub joke comes from. Like a huge steel [[@floating-ships|ship that floats]], what matters is how heavy something is for its size.

Uranus and Neptune are about four times as wide as Earth. They contain more water, ammonia and methane ice, so they are sometimes called the [[@space-weird-hot-ice|ice giants]].

{{story:big-small-scale}}

Size alone doesn't make something a planet. Jupiter's moon Ganymede and Saturn's moon [[@titan|Titan]] are both wider than the planet Mercury. Ganymede is the largest moon in the [[solar-system|solar system]].

[[@pluto|Pluto]], on the other hand, is smaller than our own Moon, which is one reason [[astronomer|astronomers]] rethought what counts as a planet.

The hardest thing to picture is [[@space-distances|how far apart the planets are]]. Suppose the Sun were a football. Earth would be a peppercorn about 24 m away. Jupiter would be a large marble about 120 m away. Neptune, the farthest planet, would be a small bead more than 700 m away, the length of a long walk through a park.

At that scale, the nearest star would be another football thousands of kilometres away. Space is mostly empty.

Even Jupiter is small next to the Sun. The [[@sun-what|Sun]] is about 109 times as wide as Earth and holds more than 99% of all the mass in the solar system. Everything else, every planet, moon, [[asteroid|asteroid]] and [[comet|comet]], is crumbs left over from the cloud that formed it about 4.6 billion years ago.

text: Yes, but so far only if they are very rich, very lucky or both. More than a hundred private passengers have now been to space, most of them on short hops that go up past 100 km, float for a few minutes and come back down.

A smaller group have gone into [[orbit|orbit]], circling Earth for days, and a few have stayed on the [[@space-station|International Space Station]]. Tickets have cost anywhere from a few hundred thousand dollars to tens of millions. In 2026, the two main companies selling short trips were both paused or rebuilding, so the queue to space is growing.

A suborbital rocket does the same thing, only 100 km up, and that hanging moment is when passengers float. Count how long your ball's "float" lasts, then picture it stretched to four minutes.

The usual edge of space is just 100 km above the ground. That is a little less than the distance from Mumbai to Pune, or from New York City to Philadelphia, except straight up.

sec.t:
In July 2021, two companies flew their founders within nine days of each other. Virgin Galactic's rocket plane was dropped from a carrier aircraft and fired its engine. Blue Origin's New Shepard rocket launched straight up from West Texas, and its capsule floated down under parachutes.

New Shepard's passengers included the actor William Shatner, aged 90, and Ed Dwight, who had trained as an astronaut candidate in the 1960s and finally flew in 2024 at 90 too. In May 2024, Gopi Thotakura, a pilot from Andhra Pradesh, became the first Indian to go to space as a tourist. In January 2026, Blue Origin paused these flights for at least two years after carrying 98 people.

Orbit is much harder than a hop. To stay up you must travel sideways at about 28,000 km/h, fast enough to cross India from top to bottom in under 10 minutes. In 2021, SpaceX flew four people with no professional astronauts aboard on a three-day orbit called Inspiration4. In 2024, a private mission called Polaris Dawn included the first spacewalk by people who were not government astronauts.

India has a strong link too. In 2025, Indian Air Force pilot Shubhanshu Shukla flew to the space station on a private mission called Axiom-4, training for India's own [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]] flights.

Passengers describe huge pressure pushing them into their seats during launch, about three times normal weight for orbital rockets. Then the engines cut out and everything floats, including pens, crumbs and stomach contents, so sick bags are standard kit. Many tourists say the strongest moment is seeing Earth's thin blue skin of air against black space.

Your body changes fast up there. Fluid moves into your head and your sense of balance gets confused, as in [[@space-body|space and the body]].

Probably, slowly. Air travel was once only for the rich too. Virgin Galactic planned to restart flights with new ships in early 2027, after a delay from late 2026, while early customers had paid $200,000 to $250,000 and newer tickets cost about $750,000. Even so, that is many lifetimes of savings for most families. A single ticket would buy a good house in most Indian cities, with change to spare.

The cheaper route may be national programmes. And if you think floating is the strangest part, wait until you see how astronauts sleep, eat and use a toilet aboard the [[@space-station|space station]].

text: In many tests, crows are as clever as great apes. They make and use tools, solve puzzles with several steps, and remember people for years. Their brains are small, about the size of a walnut, but they are crowded with brain cells. In crows and parrots, scientists found as many cells in the thinking part of [[@brain-works|the brain]] as in some monkeys.

Crows belong to a bird family called corvids, which also includes ravens, jays and magpies. In India you probably see two kinds: the grey-necked house crow and the all-black jungle crow. Both are bold, curious and very good at living around people. And like every bird, crows are a kind of dinosaur, as you can read in [[@birds-dinosaurs|how birds came from dinosaurs]].

sec.t:
In 2002, a New Caledonian crow called Betty became famous at the University of Oxford. A small bucket of food sat at the bottom of a tube. Betty was given a straight piece of wire. She bent it into a hook with her beak and fished the bucket out. Nobody had trained her to do this.

In the wild, these crows shape twigs into hooks and cut stiff leaves into barbed tools to pull insects out of holes. Few animals except humans make tools this carefully. Among [[invertebrate|invertebrates]], the [[@octopus-smart|octopus]] is a rare puzzle-solving rival.

Ravens, the crows' bigger cousins, seem to plan ahead. In a 2017 experiment in Sweden, ravens learned that a certain stone could open a box holding a treat. Later, when the box was taken away, they were offered a choice of objects. They picked the stone and kept it until the box came back, even many hours later. Planning like this was once thought to be something only humans and great apes did.

[[@urban-wildlife|City crows]] find their own solutions. In Sendai in Japan, carrion crows have been seen placing walnuts on roads so that passing cars crack them open. The birds then collect the pieces when the road is clear. Nobody taught them this. Other crows seem to have learned it by watching.

At the University of Washington in Seattle, researchers wore a scary rubber mask while catching wild crows to put rings on their legs. For years afterwards, crows scolded anyone wearing that mask, while ignoring people in other masks. Some crows that had never been caught joined in. They seemed to have learned who was dangerous from other crows.

In India, crows have long had a place in people's lives and stories. Crows appear in the [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]], and during the Hindu [[ritual|ritual]] of shraddha many families offer food to crows, believing it reaches their ancestors. A crow waiting on a wall at mealtime may be doing more thinking than it lets on.

text: A penguin's feet are kept just above freezing, at around 1 or 2°C. Not warm, just warm enough not to freeze. The trick is in the plumbing. The [[@blood|blood]] vessels carrying warm blood down into the feet run right alongside the ones bringing cold blood back up.

As the two streams pass each other, the warm blood heats the cold blood, so the heat goes back into the body instead of leaking out through the feet. Scientists call this a counter-current system. Your own [[@heart-beat|blood]] does a weaker version of the same trick in your hands and feet.
Penguins can also squeeze shut the vessels to their feet when it gets very cold, letting through only enough blood to keep the toes alive.

The wrapped cup stays colder, because the sock traps a layer of still air, just as a penguin's feathers keep the cold out and the warmth in.
myth: Penguins live at the North Pole as well as the South Pole.
Almost all wild penguins live in the southern half of the world, and none live in the Arctic. Polar bears live in the Arctic, so a penguin and a polar bear would never meet outside a zoo.

sec.t:
[[@wild-penguin-dads|Emperor penguins]] have a thick layer of fat, a few centimetres deep, under their skin. On top of that is a coat of stiff, tightly packed feathers, with fluffy down underneath that traps still air.

The coat works so well that the outer surface of the feathers can actually be colder than the air around it. Very little body heat escapes. Snow can settle on a penguin's back without melting.

Penguins spend a lot of time preening, which means combing and oiling their feathers with their beaks. The oil comes from a [[gland|gland]] near the tail and keeps the feathers [[@raincoats-waterproof|waterproof]], so [[@body-cold-swimmers|icy water]] never reaches the skin.

{{story:antarctica}}

In the Antarctic winter, it can be −40°C with fierce winds. The sun barely rises for weeks. Thousands of emperor penguins squeeze together in a huddle, packed tighter than commuters in [[@india-wonder-mumbai-local|a Mumbai local train]] at rush hour.

The huddle moves slowly, like a giant, shuffling blob. Birds on the windy edge work their way in, and birds in the middle drift out, so each one takes turns in the warm centre. Inside a tight huddle the temperature can climb above 20°C. Scientists have found that huddling saves each penguin a large share of its energy through the long winter.

In May or June, at the start of winter, the mother lays one egg and passes it carefully to the father. If it touches the ice for long, it freezes. Then she walks back to the sea to feed, sometimes many kilometres away.

The father balances the egg on his feet, under a warm fold of feathered skin called a brood pouch, for about two months. He eats nothing at all. By the time the chick hatches, he may have gone around four months without food and lost almost half his weight. If the mother is late, he can even feed the chick a milky liquid made in his throat.

Penguins can't fly in air, but they "fly" underwater with stiff wing-flippers. Emperors can [[@ocean-penguins-swim|dive deeper than 500 m]] and stay under for over 20 minutes, chasing fish, squid and krill. Their bones are solid, not hollow like those of [[@how-birds-fly|flying birds]], which helps them sink.

They need sea ice too. Emperors raise their chicks on ice joined to the coast, and in 2022 the ice broke up early at several colonies, before the chicks had grown waterproof feathers. As the world warms, scientists worry about their future, and in 2022 the USA listed them as a threatened [[species|species]]. India's Antarctic research stations, Maitri and Bharati, are among many that study the changing ice.

text: Male humpback whales sing, mostly during the winter breeding season, in warm waters where females give birth. The songs are long and complicated, made of moans, groans, squeals and whoops arranged in repeating patterns. A song can last 10 to 20 minutes, and a whale may sing it again and again for hours.

Because only males sing, and mostly when it is time to mate, scientists are sure the songs are linked to breeding. But they still argue about how. The song may attract females, a bit like a peacock's tail. It may tell other males to keep away, or help males size each other up. Some scientists suggest it could help whales locate each other in the vast ocean. The answer may be a mix of these.

sec.t:
Humpbacks don't sing the way we do. They have no vocal cords like ours, and they don't breathe out while [[@singing|singing]]. Instead, they push air back and forth inside their bodies, past a U-shaped fold in their voice box. The [[vibration|vibrations]] pass into the water through their throat and head.

Sound travels more than four times faster in water than in air, and low sounds can carry for many kilometres. Some whale sounds can probably be heard by other whales far away. To learn why water carries sound so well, read [[@sound-travel|how sound travels]].

sec.h: A hit song across the Pacific
sec.t:
In 2011, scientists published a study of humpback songs recorded across the South Pacific over more than ten years. New songs appeared near eastern Australia and then spread east, from one group of whales to the next. Within a few years, whales near French Polynesia were singing them too.

It works a bit like [[@behind-theme-music|a catchy tune]] climbing the [[@music-charts|music charts]]. Males seem to prefer something new, and when they hear it from visitors, they copy it. Scientists call this cultural transmission, meaning knowledge passed on by learning, not by [[gene|genes]].

In the 1950s, a US Navy engineer named Frank Watlington recorded strange underwater sounds near Bermuda. Later, the American scientists Roger Payne and Scott McVay studied the recordings and showed they were songs. Their paper, published in 1971, amazed the public. An [[@record-music|album]], Songs of the Humpback Whale, sold widely and helped grow the "Save the Whales" movement. In 1970, the American composer Alan Hovhaness wrote *And God Created Great Whales*, a piece for [[@orchestra|orchestra]] and recorded whale song.

Whaling had hunted humpbacks close to extinction. In 1986, a worldwide pause on commercial whaling began, and many humpback populations have grown since. Whale song was also placed on the [[@space-golden-record|golden records]] carried by the [[@voyager|Voyager]] spacecraft in 1977. In the Arabian Sea, off Oman and western India, lives a small group of humpbacks that never [[migration|migrates]], thought to be the most isolated humpback population in the world. Their songs differ from those of humpbacks elsewhere.

text: India has more wild Asian elephants than any other country, about 22,446 according to a DNA-based count released in 2025. Most live in the forests of the south and the northeast, in states like [[@karnataka|Karnataka]], Assam, Tamil Nadu and Kerala.

But India is also crowded with people, farms, roads and railways. Elephants need huge areas to find enough food and water, and their old paths now cross villages and fields. When elephants and people meet, both can get hurt. About 500 people die in encounters with elephants each year, and many elephants are killed by electric fences, trains and poisoning. Forest officers, scientists and villagers are trying new ways to help both sides live alongside each other.

Elephant corridors work the same way. When roads and fields cut them, elephants have to find new routes.
myth: Elephants that raid crops are bad-tempered "rogue" elephants.

Most crop-raiding elephants are simply hungry and following old routes through land that used to be forest. Ripe crops are easy, nutritious food. Fear, stress and being chased can make any elephant dangerous.

sec.t:
An adult Asian elephant eats around 150 kg of grass, leaves, bark and fruit a day and drinks up to about 200 litres of water. To find all that, a herd walks many kilometres, following routes passed down from older females.

These routes link forests together. Scientists call them corridors. A 2023 government report identified 150 elephant corridors across India. Many are now narrow strips squeezed between farms, towns and highways.

Elephants also shape the forest for other animals. They open paths, knock down trees to let light in and spread seeds in their dung. That's why scientists call them a [[keystone-species|keystone species]]. Many Hindus also link the elephant with Ganesha, and elephants have walked in temple festivals and royal processions for centuries. That gives many Indians a deep fondness for them, even when they are a nuisance.

[[@indian-railways|Railway]] tracks often pass through elephant corridors, especially in Assam, West Bengal and Kerala. Trains can't stop quickly, and elephants crossing at night are sometimes hit.

To reduce this, railways have marked danger zones where trains must slow down. In the northeast, a system using fibre-optic cables along the tracks can sense the heavy footsteps of elephants and warn train drivers and station staff. Some lines have underpasses and ramps so elephants can cross safely.

Some of the best ideas are simple. In Kodagu, Karnataka, a project started in 2021 hung boxes of honeybees along forest edges. Elephants seem to hate bee stings, especially around their eyes and trunks, and many turned back. A similar idea had already worked in Kenya.

In the tea and coffee estates of Valparai, in Tamil Nadu, conservationists set up an early-warning system. When someone spots elephants nearby, local people get text messages and calls, and red lights flash in the area. Since it began, deaths there have fallen sharply.

Many villagers also grow crops elephants don't like, such as chillies, lemongrass or ginger, near forest edges. Fast compensation payments for damaged crops reduce anger. There are no perfect answers, but the elephants that roam India's [[@assam-tea|tea gardens]] and coffee estates today show that people and giants can, with care, share the same land.

text: The archerfish swims just under the water's surface, watching leaves and branches above. When it spots an insect, it presses its tongue against a groove in the roof of its mouth to make a narrow tube. Then it snaps its gill covers shut, firing a jet of water out of its mouth.

The jet can reach up to about 2 m, and the fish rarely misses within a metre. The insect gets knocked into the water, and the archerfish swims in to grab it. Often the fish knows where the insect will land before it hits the surface.

sec.t:
Hitting a bug from underwater is harder than it sounds. Light bends when it moves from air into water, a process called [[refraction|refraction]]. From below, the insect isn't quite where it seems to be.

Archerfish correct for this. They seem to learn the right correction for different angles, though they often line up nearly straight below a target, where the bend is smallest. Scientists who tested them in labs found they are very accurate at many angles.

They also shoot harder at bigger insects, which cling more tightly to leaves. A small fly needs a little jet. A heavy beetle needs a strong one.

Young archerfish are bad shots. They get better with practice. In a famous 2006 study in Germany, researchers found that archerfish could learn to hit fast-moving targets just by watching other archerfish do it. Few fish are known to learn this way.

In 2016, scientists at Oxford trained archerfish to spit at photos of one human face on a screen above their tank. Shown dozens of new faces, the fish still picked out the right one most of the time. Their small brains managed a job that takes a lot of computing for machines doing [[@face-recognition|face recognition]].

Archerfish live in warm brackish water, a mix of fresh and salty, in mangrove swamps and river mouths from India across South-East Asia to northern Australia. In India, they live in the creeks of the Sundarbans, the mangrove forest shared with Bangladesh where [[@sundarbans-tigers|tigers swim]] between islands.

They don't only shoot. They also jump out of the water to snatch insects from low branches, and eat food that falls in. In some places, people keep them as aquarium pets, and they have been known to spit at lights and at their owners' faces.

Mangroves give them a perfect hunting ground. Branches hang low over the water, packed with ants, spiders, grasshoppers and beetles. It is one of the many reasons scientists say [[@insects-importance|insects]] hold up whole [[foodchain|food chains]], even underwater ones.

text: An escalator is a moving loop of steps fixed to a chain. An electric motor at the top turns gear wheels that pull the chain round and round, like the chain on a bicycle. The steps ride up one side of the loop and return underneath.

Each step has four small wheels. The front pair runs on one track, the back pair on another. On the sloping part, the two tracks are set at different heights, so the step stays level and you can stand on it. Near the top and bottom, the tracks come together. The steps flatten into a moving walkway, then tip under the floor and head back round.
A rubber handrail runs on its own loop, driven by the same motor so it moves at nearly the same speed as the steps.

st.reveal: The front wheels of each step ride on one track and the back wheels on another. On the slope, the tracks are set apart so the step stays level. At the top and bottom, the tracks come together, and the step folds flat to slide out of sight.

sec.t:
Look closely at an escalator step and you'll see deep grooves running along it. At each end, the steps slide under a metal plate with teeth like a comb, which fit into those grooves. The comb lifts your shoes off as the step disappears, so nothing gets pulled in.

That is why escalator signs warn you to step off promptly and keep loose laces and long clothes away from the edges. Yellow lines along the sides mark the gap where the step meets the wall. There's an emergency stop button at each end, usually red, that anyone can press if someone falls.

Escalators move far more people than lifts, because they never stop to wait or open doors. That makes them perfect for busy train stations. In [[@london|London]], the Underground has hundreds of them, some descending deep below the streets. Moscow's metro has some of the longest in the world, taking more than two minutes to ride.

In India, escalators are now common at metro stations in Delhi, Bengaluru and other cities, and at busy stations on [[@indian-railways|Indian Railways]]. For many people, their first escalator ride was at a mall or a new metro station, and it can feel strange at first. Holding the handrail and stepping on with a confident stride helps.

In many cities, people stand on one side and leave the other free for walkers. In London it's stand on the right. In Delhi and Mumbai, the habit varies by station.

Engineers have studied what works best. In 2015 and 2016, London tried a test at Holborn, which has a very tall escalator. Staff asked everyone to stand on both sides at rush hour. Far more people got up per minute, because the walking lane had often been half empty. On short escalators, though, walking up may still help the crowd move.

text: [[sound|Sound]] travels about 343 metres every second in air, much slower than light.

When a [[@drums|drum]] is hit, its skin wobbles back and forth. Each wobble squeezes the air next to it, then lets it spread out again. Those squeezes pass from one bit of air to the next, like a push moving through a queue of people, until they reach your ear. The air itself doesn't travel from the drum to you. Only the push does.
In water it goes over four times faster, because water [[molecule|molecules]] are packed closer together.
That's why you see lightning before you hear [[@thunder-sound|thunder]].

frames.cap: Hit a drum. Its skin wobbles back and forth very fast.
Each wobble squashes the air next to it, then lets it spread out. The squash passes from air to air, like a push through a crowd.
The squashes reach your ear and wobble your eardrum. Your brain turns that wobble into sound.
In space, there's no air to push. So space is silent!

quiz.prompt: Through which of these does sound travel fastest?
quiz.reveal: Steel, by far. Sound moves about 17 times faster through steel than through air. Its particles are packed tightly and pushed back hard when squeezed, so they pass the vibration along very quickly.

myth: Explosions in space make a huge boom, like in the movies.

Space is almost empty, with nothing to carry the squashes and stretches of a sound wave. An explosion out there would be completely silent to anyone floating nearby. Film-makers add the boom because silence feels strange to audiences.

sec.h: High and low, loud and soft
sec.t:
The number of wobbles each second is called the [[frequency|frequency]]. A fast wobble gives a high note, like a [[@whistles|whistle]]. A slow wobble gives a low note, like a big dhol. People can hear from about 20 to 20,000 wobbles a second. A [[@sitar-strings|sitar's]] thin strings shake faster than its thick ones, so they sound higher.

How hard the air is squeezed decides loudness. Loudness is measured in [[decibel|decibels]]. Quiet breathing is about 10 decibels, and a [[@plane-jet|jet engine]] close up is well over 120, loud enough to hurt your [[@ears-hear|ears]].

In Vijayapura, in Karnataka, stands [[@india-wonder-gol-gumbaz|the Gol Gumbaz]], a tomb built in the 1600s with one of the biggest domes in the world. Whisper against the wall of the gallery running round inside it, and someone on the far side can hear you clearly. The curved wall guides the sound round the edge instead of letting it spread out.

The US Capitol in Washington has a similar effect in its old hall of the House of Representatives, now called Statuary Hall. Tour guides love to show it off to visitors. In both buildings, the trick comes from the shape of the curved walls and ceiling.

In 1947, the American pilot Chuck Yeager flew the rocket plane Bell X-1 faster than the speed of sound. A plane that fast outruns its own noise. The squashed air piles up into a shock wave, heard on the ground as a sudden double bang called [[@sky-sonic-boom|a sonic boom]].

A crack of a whip is a tiny sonic boom too. The tip of the whip moves faster than sound.

When sound hits a hard surface, it bounces back as an echo. Shout towards a cliff that's 170 metres away and the echo returns in about one second. [[@echolocation|Bats]] use echoes to hunt in the dark. They send out high squeaks and listen for the echoes, building a sound picture of the moths around them.

In space, there's no air at all, so there's nothing to squeeze. Astronauts on a spacewalk talk by radio, which uses waves that don't need air. If one tapped the other's helmet with a tool, though, the sound would travel through their touching suits, because solids carry sound too.

text: A spring is a coil of springy metal, usually steel. When you squash it or stretch it, you push the metal out of its natural shape. The metal pushes back, trying to return. While you hold it squashed or stretched, it is storing the energy you put in. Scientists call this elastic [[potential-energy|potential energy]].
Let go, and the spring snaps back, releasing that energy. It might launch a toy, close a door, or push a pen nib back inside.
The spring doesn't create energy. It works like a battery for push and pull: you put energy in by bending it, and get it back later.

st.reveal: Most springs follow Hooke's law. Triple the weight, triple the stretch, as long as you don't pull so hard that the spring is bent out of shape for good.

sec.t:
In the 1600s, the English scientist Robert Hooke tested springs by hanging weights from them. He found a neat rule. If one weight stretches a spring by 2 cm, two weights stretch it by 4 cm, and three by 6 cm. The stretch grows in step with the force.

Hooke was worried rivals would steal his idea. In 1676 he published it as a jumbled set of letters, "ceiiinosssttuv". Two years later he revealed the answer, a Latin phrase *ut tensio sic vis*, meaning "as the stretch, so the force". This rule is now called Hooke's law, and it lets engineers design springs that push with exactly the force they need.

It only works up to a point. Pull too hard and the metal bends for good. That point is called the elastic limit.

In 1943, an American naval engineer named Richard James was working with springs meant to steady instruments on ships. One fell off a shelf and kept moving, flipping end over end across the floor. He and his wife Betty saw a toy in it, and Betty named it the Slinky.

In 1945, they demonstrated it at a department store in Philadelphia, and the first batch sold out quickly. Millions have been sold since. A Slinky walks downstairs because each coil passes its energy on to the next, and [[gravity|gravity]] keeps pulling it down.

Living things use springs too. When you run, the long [[tendon|tendon]] at the back of your ankle, the Achilles tendon, stretches as your foot lands and springs back as you push off. It stores energy from one step and returns some of it in the next, like a pogo stick.

Kangaroos in [[@australia|Australia]] take this further. The huge tendons in their back legs act as springs, so hopping fast costs them surprisingly little extra energy. Trampolines, car suspensions, mattresses and the springy floors used in [[@gymnastics|gymnastics]] all borrow the same trick: soak up energy on the way down, give it back on the way up.

text: X-rays are a kind of light with far more energy than the light we see. They can pass through soft parts of the body, like skin, fat and muscle, much as sunlight passes through a window.

Dense things are harder to get through. Bones are packed with calcium, so they stop many X-rays. When [[@jobs-doctor|a doctor]] takes an X-ray, a machine sends a short burst of rays through you towards a detector on the other side. Where the rays get through, the picture turns dark. Where bone blocks them, it stays pale. The result is a shadow picture of the inside of your body, with your [[@bones|bones]] shining white.

st.reveal: X-rays pass easily through skin and muscle and darken the detector behind you. Bone is dense and full of calcium, so it stops many of the rays. Where fewer rays get through, the picture stays pale, so bones show up white.

sec.t:
Doctors grabbed the new rays almost at once to find broken bones and swallowed coins. During World War One, [[@marie-curie|Marie Curie]] helped fit cars with X-ray machines so [[surgeon|surgeons]] near the front could locate bullets and shrapnel. The cars became known as "little Curies".

Early users didn't know that strong X-rays could harm living cells, and some suffered burns from long exposures. Today the doses are tiny, the beam is aimed only where needed, and staff stand behind shields. A heavy apron lined with lead may cover parts of you that don't need to be pictured. If you are ever unsure about a scan, it is fine to ask the doctor or radiographer what it is for and how it works.

An ordinary X-ray flattens everything into one shadow, so organs overlap. In the 1970s, the British engineer Godfrey Hounsfield and the American physicist Allan Cormack worked out how to take X-rays from many angles and let a computer build slices through the body. This CT scan earned them a Nobel Prize in 1979.

X-rays are also used outside [[@hospitals|hospitals]]. [[@airport-security|Airport scanners]] look through suitcases. Dentists check for holes inside teeth. Museums X-ray old paintings and find earlier pictures hidden beneath the paint. Factories X-ray [[@made-planes|metal parts of aircraft]] to look for cracks too small to see from outside, and [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] use X-rays to peer inside ancient [[@mummies|mummies]] without unwrapping them.

Hot, violent places in the universe, such as gas swirling around [[@black-holes|black holes]], give off X-rays. Earth's air blocks almost all of them, which is lucky for us but hard for [[astronomer|astronomers]]. So NASA launched the Chandra X-ray Observatory in 1999 to look from above the [[atmosphere|atmosphere]]. India's AstroSat, launched by [[@india-space-budget|ISRO]] in 2015, carries X-ray instruments as well. These telescopes have to be built very differently from ordinary ones, because X-rays go straight through a normal mirror. Instead, the rays are made to skim off curved metal surfaces at a very shallow angle, like a stone skipping across a pond.

text: The Bengal School was a group of artists, based in Kolkata from about 1900, who wanted Indian painting to look Indian again. At the time, art schools in British India mostly taught European oil painting. Abanindranath Tagore and his students turned instead to Indian stories, old Indian paintings and soft watercolours.

The movement grew alongside the freedom struggle. For many people, painting in an Indian way was a quiet form of protest. It shaped Indian art for decades and trained artists who went on to teach all over the country.

sec.t:
Abanindranath Tagore was the nephew of the poet [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]]. As a young man he learned European-style painting, but he became more interested in Mughal miniatures he saw in books and museums. In 1902 he painted *The Passing of Shah Jahan*, which shows the old emperor on his deathbed, gazing across the river at the Taj Mahal he built for his wife. It is small and sad, with fine lines and pale colours, and it showed the direction his art would take.

An unexpected supporter helped him. Ernest Binfield Havell, the British principal of the Government School of Art in Calcutta, believed Indian students were wrongly being taught to copy European art. He invited Abanindranath to teach there in 1905. Together they changed what students learned, and Havell even moved some European paintings out of the school's gallery to make room for Indian ones.

sec.h: A painting in a time of protest
Washes from Japan, ideas from Ajanta
sec.t:
In 1902, the Japanese thinker Okakura Kakuzo stayed in Kolkata with the Tagore family. The next year two Japanese painters, Yokoyama Taikan and Hishida Shunso, followed. They showed how to paint with thin layers of watery colour, letting each dry before the next. Abanindranath adopted and changed the method. His pictures often look as if seen through morning haze.

His students looked backward as well as east. Nandalal Bose and Asit Kumar Haldar travelled to copy the ancient [[mural|murals]] in the Ajanta caves, where artists had made their own [[@ajanta-colours|colours]] from earth and minerals. Their paintings show gods, poets, village women and scenes from the epics, usually in long, flowing lines.

The school's biggest influence came through its students. [[@nandalal-bose|Nandalal Bose]] went on to lead the art school at Santiniketan, called Kala Bhavana. K. Venkatappa took the style to Mysore. Abdur Rahman Chughtai, in Lahore, developed his own graceful version that is admired in Pakistan today.

Abanindranath also wrote much-loved children's books in Bengali, such as *Kheerer Putul* (The Sugar Doll), and illustrated many of them himself.

Not everyone loved the Bengal School. By the 1930s, some artists found it too soft, too sentimental and too fond of the past. Amrita Sher-Gil, who had trained in Paris, painted bold, strong figures instead. Jamini Roy turned to the bright, simple shapes of Bengal's village painters.

These arguments were part of a bigger question: what should modern Indian art look like? The Bengal School gave one of the first answers. Even artists who disagreed with it were answering the question it had asked.

sec.t:
Think of a packet of biscuits. A farmer sells wheat to a mill, the mill sells flour to a factory, the factory sells biscuits to a shop, and the shop sells them to you. GST is charged at each step, but each business gets back the tax it already paid on what it bought.

The government plans its spending in the yearly [[@budget-government|Budget]], and GST is one of its biggest sources of money. Goods brought in from abroad, or [[import|imported]], pay GST too.

The monthly GST total is also a clue about the [[economy|economy]]. When it grows fast, it often means factories are busy and shoppers are spending. Experts compare each month with the same month a year earlier, so that festival months are matched with festival months. Totals are counted in [[@lakh-crore|lakh crore]], a way to write very big numbers, and they help everyone see how [[@india-economy|India's economy]] is doing.

text: Field hockey is played by two teams of 11, each with a goalkeeper, on a rectangular pitch about the size of a football field. Players use a curved stick to dribble, pass and hit a hard ball into the other team's goal. A match has four quarters of 15 minutes, and the team with more goals wins.

What makes hockey different from football is the stick. You may only touch the ball with the flat face of the stick, not the rounded back, and outfield players can't kick it. Goals count only if an attacker touches the ball inside the shooting circle, a semicircle in front of each goal.

sec.t:
A hockey stick is flat on one side and rounded on the other, with a hooked end. Players hold it with the flat side facing the ball. Using the rounded side is a foul. To move the ball to their left, skilled players flip the stick over with a quick twist of the wrists.

The ball is solid plastic, about the size of a cricket ball but harder and smoother. On modern artificial pitches, which are watered before games to make the surface fast, it can be hit at well over 100 km/h. Players wear shin guards and mouth guards. Goalkeepers wear helmets and big padded kickers, and they are the only players allowed to use their feet or body in their own circle.

The most exciting set piece is the penalty corner. It is given when defenders foul inside their own circle, or sometimes just outside it. An attacker pushes the ball from the back line to teammates waiting at the top of the circle.

Up to five defenders, including the goalkeeper, rush out from the goal to block it. The attackers stop the ball and then shoot, or "drag-flick" it, slinging it towards goal in one smooth movement. Top drag-flickers like India's Harmanpreet Singh score many of their team's goals this way. A penalty stroke, a one-on-one shot from a spot 6.4 metres out, is given for fouls that stop a likely goal.

Modern field hockey rules were drawn up in England in the 1800s, and the game spread through the British Empire. India took to it brilliantly. Between 1928 and 1956, India's men won six Olympic gold medals in a row, led for many years by the great [[@dhyan-chand|Dhyan Chand]]. They won two more, in 1964 and 1980.

When the game moved from grass to artificial turf in the 1970s, faster, more physical styles took over, and India struggled for decades. In Tokyo in 2021, the men won bronze, their first Olympic medal in 41 years. They won bronze again in Paris in 2024. The women's team reached the semi-finals in Tokyo, finishing fourth.

In the United States and Canada, "hockey" usually means ice hockey. It is played on skates, with six players a side, a flat rubber disc called a puck and sticks with a flat blade. Players can bump into each other, and the game is very fast.

Field hockey in the US is mostly played by women and girls in schools and colleges, though the national teams include both men and women. Both games share a stick, a goal and a love of speed. Like the [[@cricket-rules|rules of cricket]], the rules of each have been tweaked over the years to keep matches fair and exciting, and the [[@umpires-referees|umpires]] have plenty to watch.

text: Food gives your body three big kinds of [[nutrient|nutrients]]: [[carbohydrate|carbohydrates]], [[protein|proteins]] and fats. Each has its own main job.

Carbohydrates, or carbs, are mostly fuel. Rice, roti, potatoes and fruit are full of them. Your body breaks them into sugar, which your cells burn for energy. Proteins are building material. Dal, eggs, milk, [[@cheese-paneer|paneer]], fish and meat give your body the pieces it needs to build muscle, skin, hair and much else. Fats are a store of energy and a building material too. They form the outer skin of every cell and help your body take in some [[vitamin|vitamins]]. A healthy diet mixes all three.

st.reveal: Ghee is almost pure fat, and fat holds about 9 kilocalories a gram. Sugar is a carbohydrate, with about 4. Paneer is a mix of protein, fat and quite a lot of water, so gram for gram it holds less energy than either.

sec.t:
When you eat rice or [[@wheat-bread|bread]], your gut breaks the [[starch|starch]] down into a sugar called glucose. It passes into your [[@blood|blood]] and travels to every cell. Your brain runs almost entirely on glucose, using about a fifth of all your body's energy, even though it weighs only about 2% of your body.

Some carbs, like white sugar, are absorbed very fast. Others, like whole grains, [[@millets|millets]] and beans, break down slowly and keep you going longer. Fibre is a carb you can't digest at all, but your gut [[microbe|microbes]] feed on it and it keeps your [[digestion|digestion]] moving.

sec.h: Fats: the store and the wall
sec.t:
Fat holds about twice as much energy per gram as carbs or protein. That makes it the body's long-term store, packed under the skin and around the organs. It also keeps you warm and cushions your organs.

Every cell in your body is wrapped in a thin skin made largely of fat. Your brain is about 60% fat by dry weight. Some fats, called essential fatty acids, can't be made by the body and must come from food, such as nuts, seeds, mustard oil and fish.

The energy in food is measured in kilocalories, often just called calories. One kilocalorie is the energy needed to warm one litre of water by one degree Celsius. In the late 1800s, an American chemist named Wilbur Atwater burned foods in sealed containers and measured the heat. He also measured what people ate and what left their bodies. His numbers, 4 for carbs and protein and 9 for fat, are still printed on food labels today.

A balanced [[@thali|thali]] does a neat job of all this: rice or roti for fuel, dal and curd for protein, a little ghee or oil, and vegetables for vitamins and fibre. India's [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]] scheme in schools is planned around similar ideas, to give children enough energy and protein each school day.

text: A baby starts when one egg cell from the mother joins with one sperm cell from the father. That single cell divides again and again, becoming a tiny ball of cells that grows into a baby. Twins happen in two different ways.

Sometimes, in the first days, that tiny ball of cells splits into two. Each half grows into a whole baby. These are identical twins. They come from the same egg and sperm, so they share the same [[gene|genes]]. Other times, the mother releases two eggs at once, and each one is joined by a different sperm. Two separate babies grow side by side. These are non-identical twins, also called fraternal twins. They are as alike as any brother and sister, just born on the same day.

options.t: No, boy-girl twins are always non-identical

st.reveal: Identical twins come from one fertilised egg, so they share the same genes, including those that decide whether a baby is a boy or a girl. Boy-girl twins must have come from two different eggs, so they are non-identical.

sec.t:
Identical twins are always both boys or both girls, and they usually look very alike. Even so, they aren't copies. Their [[@fingerprints|fingerprints]] differ. One may be left-handed and the other right-handed. They can have different heights, likes and personalities.

That's because genes aren't the only thing that shapes a person. Small differences in the womb, different experiences and pure chance all play a part. Some identical twins are [[@mirrors|mirror]] images. One twin's hair may swirl clockwise and the other's anticlockwise, or a birthmark may sit on opposite sides.

Twin births have become more common over the last 50 years in many countries, including the USA. One reason is that more women are having babies when they're older, and older mothers are more likely to release two eggs at once. Another is fertility treatment, which can lead to more than one baby.

Triplets, quadruplets and more can also happen, from extra eggs, extra splits or both. Nine-banded armadillos, which live from South America to the southern USA, almost always have four identical babies from one split egg. The ancient Greeks named the [[constellation|constellation]] Gemini, meaning twins, after the twin brothers Castor and Pollux, and you can find it among the [[@constellations|constellations]] on winter nights.

Because identical twins share genes, scientists study them to learn what genes do and what the world around us does. If identical twins are much more alike in something than non-identical twins, genes probably play a big part.

In 2015, astronaut Scott Kelly spent nearly a year on the International [[@space-station|Space Station]], while his identical twin, Mark, also an astronaut, stayed on Earth. NASA scientists compared their bodies before, during and after. They found changes in Scott's genes' activity, his eyes and his gut [[microbe|microbes]], most of which went back to normal on Earth.

text: Every app you use has been carefully planned by designers. They decide where buttons go, how big they are, what colours to use and what happens when you tap. Their job is to make the app feel obvious, so that you can use it without reading instructions.

Many apps look alike because their designers have learned the same lessons. Fingers are fat and screens are small, so buttons must be big enough to hit. People's thumbs rest near the bottom of a phone, so important buttons move there. Users expect certain symbols, like a magnifying glass for search, so designers rarely change them. Apple and Google also publish detailed guides that most designers follow.

st.reveal: As phones grew bigger, the top corners became hard to reach with one hand. Many apps moved their main buttons into a bar along the bottom, inside the zone your thumb can sweep across.

sec.h: Buttons that ask to be pressed
sec.t:
In his book *The Design of Everyday Things*, the American scientist Don Norman wrote about objects that show you how to use them. A door handle you can grab says "pull". A flat metal plate says "push". The same idea works on screens.

A button with a shape, a colour or a shadow looks pressable. Plain grey text does not. Designers also give feedback: a button changes colour when tapped, or the phone gives a tiny buzz. Without that, people tap again and again, wondering whether anything happened.

Some icons have outlived the things they show. The "save" button in many programs is still a floppy disk, though most children have never seen one. A phone handset means "call", even on phones shaped like slabs of glass.

The three-line menu icon, often called the hamburger, was drawn by designer Norm Cox for the Xerox Star computer in 1981. It vanished for years and came back with smartphones. Designers keep familiar symbols because changing them confuses millions of people at once. Road signs work the same way: their shapes and [[@fonts|fonts]] change very slowly, because drivers must read them in a split second.

Good design works for people who see, hear or move differently. About one in 12 men has some [[@colour-blindness|colour blindness]], usually trouble telling red from green. So designers don't rely on colour alone. An error message might be red and also carry a warning symbol.

Text must contrast strongly with its background so people with weak eyesight can read it. Apps should work with screen readers, which read out what is on the screen for blind users. In India, many apps offer several languages and scripts, and some use clear icons for people who are just learning to read.

Big companies test designs on real people. In an A/B test, half the users see one version and half see another, and the company measures which one people use more. Even the shade of a button can be tested.

Not every trick is kind. Some apps use "dark patterns": designs that push you into things you didn't mean to do, like a tiny "no thanks" link or an endless scroll that's hard to stop. Knowing how [[@apps-made|apps are made]] helps you spot when a design is working for you, and when it's working on you.

text: Princely states were kingdoms inside British India that were ruled by Indian princes, not by British officials. In 1947 there were about 565 of them. Together they covered around two-fifths of the land of undivided India.

The princes accepted Britain as the supreme power. The British controlled their defence and their dealings with the outside world, and kept an official called a Resident at many courts. Inside their states, the rulers collected taxes, made laws and lived in grand palaces. When the British left in 1947, the princes had to decide whether to join India or Pakistan. Almost all joined one or the other within two years.

st.prompt: How big was the smallest princely state?
st.reveal: Princely states ranged from Hyderabad, bigger than many European countries, down to tiny estates in Gujarat and elsewhere that covered only a handful of villages. Some rulers had fewer subjects than a large school has pupils.

sec.t:
The states came in every size. Hyderabad, ruled by the Nizam, was larger than England and Scotland together. [[@kashmir|Jammu and Kashmir]] was even bigger in area. Mysore, Baroda, Travancore and Gwalior were also large and rich.

At the other end were tiny states, especially in Gujarat's Kathiawar region, that were little more than a few villages. The British ranked rulers by gun salutes. The most important received 21 guns when they visited a British official. Smaller rulers got fewer, and some got none, which they took as an insult.

When independence came, the British said the princes could join India or Pakistan, or in theory stay independent. A patchwork of hundreds of independent kingdoms would have made a united India very hard to run.

[[@sardar-patel|Sardar Patel]], India's Home Minister, and his secretary V.P. Menon set out to persuade the rulers. They offered an Instrument of Accession: the princes would hand over defence, foreign affairs and communications, and keep their titles, palaces and a yearly allowance called a privy purse. Through meetings, appeals to patriotism and some firm pressure, most rulers signed before 15 August 1947.

A few states held out. The Nawab of Junagadh, in Gujarat, joined Pakistan, though most of his people were Hindu and the state was surrounded by India. Indian forces moved in, and a vote in February 1948 showed most people wanted to join India.

The Nizam of Hyderabad wanted independence. After long talks failed and violence grew inside the state, the Indian Army entered in September 1948 in an operation lasting a few days, and Hyderabad joined India. In Jammu and Kashmir, Maharaja Hari Singh joined India in October 1947 after an invasion by tribal fighters from Pakistan. The region's status has been disputed between India and Pakistan ever since.

Over the next few years, the old states were merged into new [[@states-india|Indian states]], such as Rajasthan, which joined together more than twenty princely states. Many rulers became governors, ministers or members of Parliament. Their old forts, like the great [[@rajasthan-forts|hill forts of Rajasthan]], passed into the care of the new government or stayed with royal families.

In 1971, a constitutional [[amendment|amendment]] ended the privy purses and royal titles. Many palaces became hotels, museums or family homes. In [[@jaipur|Jaipur]], Udaipur and Mysuru, visitors can now walk through rooms where kings once held court.

text: The USA is about three times the size of India, and its land changes a lot as you cross it. On the east coast there are low, worn-down mountains. In the middle there are flat grasslands so wide that the horizon looks like the sea. Then the land rises sharply into the [[@rocky-mountains|Rocky Mountains]], falls into deserts and rises again before reaching the Pacific Ocean.

From New York to Los Angeles is about 4,000 km in a straight line, and more by road. Driving it, with stops to eat and sleep, takes about four days. Along the way you would cross four time zones and set your watch back three hours.

sec.t:
The Atlantic coast is low and flat, with long beaches, marshes and big harbours. That is why the early cities, such as Boston, New York and Philadelphia, grew there. Inland rise the [[@appalachians|Appalachian Mountains]]. They are some of the oldest mountains on Earth, formed hundreds of millions of years ago. Rain and wind have rounded them so much that their highest peak is just over 2,000 m.

Further north are the five [[@great-lakes|Great Lakes]], shared with Canada. Together they hold about a fifth of all the fresh water lying on Earth's surface.

Then the Rocky Mountains rise like a wall. They are much younger than the Appalachians, so their peaks are still sharp and many pass 4,000 m. Along their spine runs the Continental Divide. Rain falling on one side flows towards the Atlantic, and on the other side towards the Pacific.

Beyond the Rockies lies dry, high land with [[@earth-salt-flats|salt flats]], red rock and canyons. The Colorado River cut the [[@grand-canyon|Grand Canyon]] here. Much of this country is protected in [[@national-parks|national parks]], so its strange shapes stay wild.

Close to the west coast stand more mountains, the [[@yosemite|Sierra Nevada]] and the Cascades. They catch rain from the Pacific, so the land behind them is very dry. This is where you find [[@mystery-sailing-stones|Death Valley]], the hottest and [[@extreme-lowest-point|lowest place]] in North America. In summer it can pass 50 °C.

The Pacific coast itself is cooler, often foggy, and sits on top of active faults, which is why California has so many [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]]. Its Central Valley is one of the richest farming areas in the world. A large share of the almonds, grapes and tomatoes eaten in the USA grows there, watered by snow melting off the mountains.

Two states are not joined to the rest. [[@alaska|Alaska]], in the far north-west, holds Denali, the tallest mountain in North America. [[@hawaii-islands|Hawaii]] is a chain of volcanic islands in the middle of the Pacific. Add them in and the USA stretches across six [[@time-zones|time zones]]. Compare that with [[@india-geography|India]], which runs all its clocks on a single time.

text: The Navajo code talkers were Native American Marines who sent [[@words-secret-languages|secret radio messages]] for the United States during the Second World War. They used a code built on their own language, Navajo, which very few outsiders could speak.

A short message that took a coding machine about half an hour could be sent by a pair of code talkers in well under a minute. The Japanese forces in the Pacific listened in constantly. They never broke it.

st.prompt: In the Navajo code, what did the word for "iron fish" mean?
st.reveal: Navajo had no words for modern weapons, so the code talkers invented them. A submarine became "iron fish", a tank became "tortoise" and a fighter plane became "hummingbird".

The code was built on Navajo, but it used invented words and spelled-out letters. A Navajo speaker without the training heard only strange lists of animals and objects.

sec.t:
By 1942 the enemy had become good at cracking codes made from numbers and letters. A spoken language was harder. Navajo has complex grammar and sounds that are hard for outsiders to hear correctly, and a small change in tone can change a word's meaning.

It also had almost no written form at the time, so there were no [[@dictionaries|dictionaries]] for an enemy to study. The idea came from Philip Johnston, the son of a missionary, who had grown up on the [[@navajo-nation|Navajo reservation]] in the American Southwest and spoke the language.

Code talkers served in every major Marine battle in the Pacific from 1942 to 1945. They worked in pairs, one speaking into a field [[@radio-waves|radio]] and one listening, often under fire. In the first two days of the battle of Iwo Jima in 1945, six code talkers sent more than 800 messages without a single mistake.

They were not the only Native code talkers. Choctaw soldiers had sent messages in their language in the [[@world-war-one|First World War]], and Comanche soldiers did so in Europe during the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], including on D-Day.

sec.h: A language that was nearly lost
sec.t:
Many code talkers had gone to government boarding schools that tried to make Native children give up their languages. Some were punished for speaking Navajo. The irony was not lost on them.

The code stayed a military secret until 1968, so for over 20 years the men could not tell even their families what they had done. Recognition came slowly. In 1982 the US named 14 August National Navajo Code Talkers Day, and in 2001 the original 29 received the Congressional Gold Medal. Chester Nez, the last of that first group, died in 2014.

The story is now one of the best-known examples of how a language carries knowledge nobody else has. Navajo is still spoken by well over 100,000 people, which makes it one of the strongest Native languages in the United States. Many others are far closer to vanishing, as you can read in [[@endangered-languages|endangered languages]]. Each one that survives keeps a way of naming the world that no [[cipher|cipher]] could copy.

text: Native American stories explain how the world was made, why animals look the way they do, and how people should treat each other and the land. They star [[trickster|tricksters]], heroes, spirits and talking animals.

But there is no single set of "Native American myths". Before Europeans arrived, North America was home to hundreds of nations, each with its own language and its own stories. Today the USA recognises 574 tribal nations (as of 2025), and Canada has hundreds more First Nations. Many stories are still told, often by elders, and some are sacred and shared only within a community.

sec.h: A world on a turtle's back
sec.t:
The Haudenosaunee (sometimes called the Iroquois) tell of Sky Woman, who fell through a hole in the sky world. Below her was only water. Birds caught her on their wings, and a great turtle offered its back as a resting place.

The animals dived to find mud from the bottom. Many failed. At last, a small muskrat came up nearly drowned, with a pawful of mud. Sky Woman spread it on the turtle's shell, and it grew into the land. That is why many Native people call North America Turtle Island.

The Cherokee have a different start: a little water beetle dives down and brings up the mud that becomes the Earth.

Almost every region has a trickster. In much of the West, it is Coyote: greedy, boastful and always getting into trouble. Sometimes his mistakes make the world better by accident. In some stories, he scatters the stars across the sky in a careless hurry, which is why they don't form neat patterns.

On the Pacific coast, the trickster is Raven, who stole daylight from a selfish chief. Among the Lakota, it is Iktomi, a shape-shifting spider. In the Southeast, it is Rabbit, a clever animal much like Br'er Rabbit of African American folk tales.

Tricksters will remind Indian readers of the clever jackals and crows of the [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]]. Stories everywhere seem to love a small animal outwitting a big one.

{{story:panchatantra-tales}}

Native storytelling often has rules about when and how stories are shared. Among the Navajo, Coyote stories are told only in winter. One reason given is that animals and spirits are asleep then and won't overhear.

Some stories belong to a particular family or clan. Others are sacred and are told only during ceremonies. That is why many Native communities ask outsiders to treat their stories with care, and why some well-known retellings in books were written down without permission.

Many nations read stories in the night sky. The Mi'kmaq of the northeast see the bowl of the Big Dipper as a bear, chased across the sky all year by seven hunter birds. Several peoples tell of seven sisters or seven children who became the Pleiades, the same cluster Indian [[astronomer|astronomers]] call the Krittika. You can see how different peoples drew different pictures among the stars in [[@constellations|constellations]].

Grandmother Spider appears in Cherokee, Hopi and other traditions. In one Cherokee story, she carries fire to the people in a little clay pot on her back. In the Southwest, stories describe Corn Mother, who gave people maize, the crop that fed much of the Americas.

Many of these stories live in their own languages, and more than 150 Native languages are still spoken in the USA. Several are in danger of disappearing, and tribes now run schools and apps to teach them to children.

One of those languages once helped win a war. During the Second World War, Navajo speakers sent military messages in their own language, and enemy codebreakers never cracked it. The story of the [[@code-talkers|code talkers]] is one of the most surprising of the 20th century.

text: Paper was invented in [[@china-today|China]]. For a long time, people gave the credit to Cai Lun, an official at the emperor's court, who presented a method for making paper in 105 CE. He used tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets.

[[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] have since found paper in China that is a few hundred years older than Cai Lun. So papermaking probably grew slowly, with Cai Lun improving it and making it official. From China, paper travelled to Korea, Japan, Central Asia, the Arab world, India and finally Europe.

st.prompt: Which creature makes its own paper?
st.reveal: Paper wasps scrape tiny bits of wood from fences and dead trees, chew them with saliva and spread the pulp into thin sheets. The grey, papery nests work on the same idea as human paper, with plant fibres matted together.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, paper and Cai Lun.

src.Dard Hunter, Papermaking: The History and Technique of an Ancient Craft (1947).

n.certNote: Old Chinese histories credit a court official, Cai Lun, with inventing paper in 105 CE. But archaeologists have found older scraps of paper in China, so most historians now say he improved papermaking rather than inventing it.

myth: The ancient Egyptians invented paper, because they wrote on papyrus.

Papyrus is made by laying strips of a plant stem crosswise and pressing them. Paper is made from fibres broken down in water and matted into a thin sheet. The word paper comes from papyrus, but the inventions are different.

sec.t:
Paper is a thin sheet made of plant fibres. To make it, the plant material is soaked and beaten until the fibres separate. They float in water like a thin soup. A papermaker dips a fine screen into the soup and lifts it out. The water drains away, and the fibres are left behind in a tangled mat. When it dries, the fibres hold together, and you have a sheet.

That is different from papyrus in Egypt, palm leaves in India, or parchment in Europe, which was made from animal skin. Those were written on for centuries, but none of them is paper.

Paper reached Central Asia along the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]]. A famous story says that Chinese papermakers were captured at the Battle of Talas in 751 and taught the craft in Samarkand. Historians doubt this tale, because paper was probably already known in the region. But Samarkand did become famous for its paper.

By the late 700s, Baghdad had [[@paper-made|paper mills]]. The Arab world made huge amounts of paper, which helped books and learning spread. Paper reached Spain with Arab rulers, and by the 1100s it was being made at Xàtiva, near Valencia. From there it spread across Europe, ready for the [[@printing-press|printing press]] in the 1450s.

In India, paper became common during the time of the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]], in the 1200s and 1300s, though palm leaves and birch bark were still used for long after. Towns like Sanganer near [[@jaipur|Jaipur]] and Kalpi in Uttar Pradesh became known for handmade paper, and some still make it.

For centuries, paper in Europe was made from old cotton and linen rags. As more people learned to read and newspapers grew, there weren't enough rags.

In 1719, the French scientist René de Réaumur wrote that wasps make paper from wood, and suggested people try it. In the 1840s, inventors in Germany and Canada finally worked out how to grind wood into pulp for paper. That made paper cheap enough for daily newspapers, schoolbooks and, eventually, toilet paper.

Today most [[@paper-made|paper]] comes from wood pulp, and much of it is [[@recycling|recycled]]. Each time paper is recycled, the fibres get shorter, so the same fibres can only be reused a handful of times. Some papermakers in India still use cotton rags, the way their ancestors did.

text: For most of history, the world's black pepper and green cardamom came mainly from one place: the hot, rainy hills and coast of south-west India. People everywhere else wanted them, and the only way to get them was by long, risky sea and land journeys.

Every trader along the way added a price. By the time a sack of pepper reached a market in Venice or London, it could cost many times what a farmer in Kerala had been paid. Pepper earned the nickname [[@food-pepper-black-gold|"black gold"]]. Cardamom, with its sweet, cooling smell, became known as the "queen of spices", with pepper as the king. Rulers, sailors and companies fought to control where they came from.

st.prompt: Black pepper, white pepper and green pepper. How many different plants do they come from?
st.reveal: All three come from the same climbing vine. Green pepper is the unripe berry kept fresh, black pepper is the unripe berry dried in the sun, and white pepper is the seed with its outer skin taken off.

sec.t:
Pepper is a climbing vine. In [[@kerala|Kerala]], farmers grow it up tall trees, and pick its small berries in clusters that look like green bunches of grapes. Dried in the sun on mats, the berries turn black and wrinkled.

Cardamom is a leafy plant of the [[@ginger-garlic|ginger family]] that likes shade, cool mist and lots of rain. It grows wild in the forests of the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], in a range still called the Cardamom Hills. Its pods sprout near the ground on long shoots, and each one must be picked by hand when it is just ripe.

For centuries, Arab and Venetian merchants controlled the spice trade into Europe. Other countries wanted to cut them out. In 1492, [[@columbus|Columbus]] sailed west hoping to reach Asia and its spices, and bumped into the Americas instead.

Vasco da Gama of Portugal tried the other way, around Africa. In 1498 his ships reached Kozhikode, then called Calicut. The Portuguese, then the Dutch and the British, all built forts and trading posts in India. The [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] began as a group of London merchants chasing spices and ended up ruling much of the country.

Pepper's bite comes from a chemical called piperine. It tickles the same heat [[sensor|sensors]] in your mouth that chillies do, though more gently. Chillies themselves only reached India from the Americas in the 1500s, so for most of history pepper was what made Indian food hot.

Cardamom's smell comes from oils inside its tiny black seeds. They fade quickly once ground, which is why many cooks crush the pods fresh for [[@food-chai-history|chai]] or kheer. In Sweden and Finland, cardamom buns are a favourite treat, so a spice from Kerala's misty hills ends up in a Nordic bakery.

India no longer leads the world in either spice. [[@vietnam|Vietnam]] now grows the most pepper, and Guatemala grows the most cardamom. Guatemala's crop began in the early 1900s, when a coffee planter brought in cardamom plants.

Kerala still grows both, and its pepper is still famous. The Spices Board, a government body, runs auctions where traders bid on sacks of cardamom. The prices change every day, as they have since Roman ships waited for the [[monsoon|monsoon]].

text: Your body needs salt because it needs sodium, one of the two things salt is made of. Sodium helps [[@nervous-system|nerves]] send electrical signals, so your brain can talk to your muscles. It helps your muscles, including your heart, squeeze. It also helps control how much water stays in your blood and cells.

You lose some sodium every day in sweat and urine, so you must replace it. But the body needs only a little. Most people eat far more than they need, mostly from packaged and restaurant food. Too much salt over many years can raise blood pressure, which strains the heart.

st.prompt: Why does most salt sold in India have iodine added to it?

options.t: To prevent goitre and other problems caused by too little iodine
To keep salt from getting damp

st.reveal: The thyroid gland in your neck needs iodine to make hormones that control growth and energy. Many soils, especially in mountain areas, have little iodine, so people can go short. Adding it to salt, which almost everyone eats, is a cheap fix.

n.certNote: Why the body needs salt is well understood. The popular story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt, giving us the word "salary", is uncertain. The Latin word is related to salt, but historians have found little proof of salt wages.

myth: Pink Himalayan salt is far healthier than ordinary salt.
Pink salt is about 98% sodium chloride, just like white salt. Its colour comes from traces of iron and other minerals, in amounts too small to make a difference. It usually has no added iodine.

sec.t:
The World Health Organization advises adults to eat less than 5 g of salt a day, about one level teaspoon. Worldwide, adults eat about twice that on average. Children need even less, depending on their size.

Your [[@kidneys|kidneys]] do the balancing. If you eat a salty snack, you feel [[@thirst|thirsty]], drink water, and your kidneys flush the extra sodium out. That's also why [[@sweat|sweat]] tastes salty: it carries sodium out of your skin. Athletes and labourers working in the heat sometimes need extra salt to replace what they lose.

Most salt comes from the sea. Seawater is about 3.5% salt, which is why the [[@why-sea-salty|sea tastes salty]]. In shallow pans near the coast, sunshine evaporates the water and leaves salt behind. In the Little [[@gujarat-rann|Rann of Kutch]] in Gujarat, families called Agariyas pump [[@groundwater|salty groundwater]] into pans and rake the crystals by hand through the dry season.

Salt is also mined from underground layers left by ancient seas that dried up. The Khewra mine in Pakistan produces the pinkish rock salt sold as "Himalayan salt". In the USA, huge salt mines lie beneath Michigan, Ohio and Louisiana, and the Great Salt Lake in Utah is several times saltier than the ocean.

Before fridges, salt was one of the best ways to keep food. Germs need water, and salt pulls water out of food and out of the germs themselves. Indian [[@pickles-achar|pickles]], [[@fishing-boats|dried fish]] on the Konkan coast and salted meat on old sailing ships all relied on it.

Salt was so valuable that it was traded across deserts and taxed by kings in many lands. The word "salary" comes from the Latin *salarium*, which is related to salt. Some say Roman soldiers were paid in salt, but historians have found little evidence for that.

In parts of India, especially the Himalayan foothills, many people once had goitre, a swelling of the thyroid [[gland|gland]] in the neck caused by too little iodine. Iodine shortage can also slow children's growth and learning.

India began a national programme to fight it in 1962, and by the 1990s most salt sold for eating had to be iodised. A packet of ordinary iodised salt from a corner shop is one of the cheapest health measures in the world.

text: India grows more kinds of spices than almost anywhere else, and has done so for thousands of years. [[@cardamom-pepper|Black pepper]] and cardamom grow wild in the hills of Kerala. Turmeric, ginger and long pepper are ancient Indian crops. When a spice is right outside your door, you cook with it.

But there is more to it than nearby supply. Spices add smell, colour and heat, and Indian cooks learned to layer many of them in one dish, each in its own way. Some are roasted, some fried in oil, some ground with water into a paste, some sprinkled on at the end. India is now the world's biggest producer, user and exporter of spices, according to the Spices Board of India.

st.prompt: Indian cooks often fry whole spices in hot oil or ghee before adding anything else. Why?

options.t: Many flavour chemicals in spices dissolve in fat, so frying spreads them through the dish
Hot oil removes the bitter skins of seeds
It makes the spices less strong

st.reveal: Many of the chemicals that give spices their smell mix with fat far better than with water. A quick fry, called tadka or tempering, pulls them out into the oil, which then carries flavour into every spoonful.

sec.t:
In the 1990s, two American scientists studied thousands of recipes from dozens of countries. They found that recipes from hotter countries, like India and [[@thailand|Thailand]], tended to use more spices than those from cold ones, like Norway.

Their explanation was that many spices kill [[bacteria|bacteria]]. In a hot place without fridges, food spoils fast, so spicy recipes might have helped people stay healthy. It is a neat idea, and lab tests show that garlic, onion and some spices do slow germs. But many scientists point out that the amounts used in cooking are small, and that history, trade and taste explain a lot too.

An Indian dish often has spice added at several moments. Whole seeds such as cumin or mustard go first into hot oil and crackle, the step called tadka. Ground spices are cooked with onions until the oil separates. A pinch of garam masala, a blend of warm spices like cinnamon, cloves and cardamom, is stirred in at the end.

Each region has its own favourites. Kashmir loves fennel and dried ginger. Bengal uses a five-seed mix called panch phoron. Kerala's curries are rich with [[@food-pepper-black-gold|black pepper]] and [[@curry-leaves|curry leaves]]. That variety is why "Indian food" tastes so different from one state to the next.

sec.h: Smell does most of the work
sec.t:
Your tongue can sense only a few basic tastes, such as sweet, salty and sour. Most of what you call "flavour" is really smell, drifting up the back of your throat to your [[@nose-smell|nose]]. Spices are packed with smelly oils, which is why a kitchen fills with aroma long before the food is ready.

That also explains a strange fact: with a heavy cold, a rich [[@biryani|biryani]] can taste of almost nothing. Chilli is the exception. Its burn is felt by pain nerves, so you notice it even with a blocked nose. Chillies came to India only about 500 years ago, as you can read in [[@chillies|the chilli's journey]].
